doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Holman's Metropole Orchestra recording and arts funding
summary: Konitz praises the Holman piece, then they talk about the orchestra's funding and the NEA.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: You didn’t get to hear any of that Holman thing?
Oh, yes. I listened to it last night, it’s terrific.
I’m a Holman fan and that instantly became up there among my favorite Holman pieces.

And they won’t release it. I cannot understand that. He was certainly a favorite of that orchestra. They release Elvis Costello records and whatever. Well that’s a different thing. Vince Mendoza is the man in charge now. He’s a fine writer also.
Yes. It’s wonderful playing, it’s wonderful writing, you sound great on it, I mean, there’s nothing not to like. It’s really inventive writing.
That’s the best in and out of [the] jazz and classical connection that I’ve heard. It’s absolutely seamless I think.
Yeah, totally. They’re in trouble now anyway you know. The Metropole, the Dutch politicians, are looking to pull the plug on them.
I talked to a lead trumpet player, a lovely guy, and he said it wouldn’t be until [two thousand] fourteen or fifteen and he doubts that they’ll cut it loose.
It’s like the politicians there are like the politicians here. They have to make noise over something, to make threats until people get in their face and make them back off.
Today’s paper says that Bloomberg is contributing some thirty-two million dollars to the arts.
I didn’t have my reading glasses on so I couldn’t see. I was looking to see if [the] National Endowment was in there but [it’s] probably the Grammys. Pop music.
Yeah, the Grammys need Bloomberg’s money. The Republicans are trying to pull the plug on the NEA right now.

Yeah, that’s the latest Republican “throwing a piece of raw meat to their base” bid. They’re trying to either eliminate the NEA [or] eliminate PBS. It’s a Chinese curse. We live in interesting times. Let’s talk about the “Half Note” records with you, Warne, Bill Evans, Jimmy Garrison, and Paul Motian. February of fifty-nine.
